hero.heading: Loren's Body Shop, a cost model sent for correction
hero.caption: Built October 4, 2026, from lorensbodyshop.com, the trade press, the industry's billing survey, and federal data. Every number is labeled: published, federal, or our assumption. The assumptions are sliders; move them and the number moves.
hero.liveCaption: The model's estimate, on the assumptions you have set below
hero.subline: (exact: $2,911 and $32,342) Under $5,000 a figure rounds to the nearest $1,000, above it to the nearest $5,000; the exact figures govern.

model.heading: Move our assumptions
model.intro: Each slider is one of the assumptions in our letter, set to the range we wrote down. If you know a figure, narrow its range, or close both handles on the exact number. The estimate above then follows your figures instead of ours. Tap a figure to type it exactly.

volume.label: Repairs you complete in a year
volume.caption: Optional. Type your volume and every dollar figure on this page scales to your year. Leave it empty and the model stays per hundred repairs.

sliders.label: Not-included operations performed and never billed, per repair
Months between estimate and parts order
sliders.basis: Half a month to two months, about two to eight weeks. Assumed, printed to be corrected [[ASSUMED]].

constants.text: Federal series: BLS producer price index, motor vehicle parts (WPU1412), 145.456 in October 2025 to 149.359 in August 2026, its latest published month: up 2.7 percent over ten months, 0.27 percent per month [[BENCHMARK]]. The model applies it only across the weeks between estimate and parts order. Next release October 15, 2026; this page changes with it.

terms.label: Parts drift between estimate and order

model.formulaText: Moved per 100 repairs = 100 × unbilled operations per repair × value per operation + 100 × short-paid share × short pay + 100 × parts per repair × months of lag × (149.359 ÷ 145.456 minus 1) ÷ 10
model.plainText: In words, the not-included operations your shop performs and never writes, plus what insurers short pay, plus what parts prices add while an estimate waits for its parts order.
model.callout: What nobody counts is the line you never wrote. The industry's own quarterly survey of 473 shops says it plainly: most shops that put a not-included operation on the estimate are paid for it most of the time, and one shop in five never asks at all. Nearly half never bill the final verification of measurements; two thirds never bill stall cure time. For a shop that works inside insurer programs, as yours does, those are not negotiations lost; they are lines that never existed.

smallRound.note: Under $5,000, a figure rounds to the nearest $1,000.

respect.heading: What you already show in the open
paragraphs: Your family opened the shop in 1951; the second generation took it in 1975; you started in 1985 and took the responsibility in 2000 [[OBSERVED]].
I-CAR Gold Class. A lifetime warranty on the repair. Seventeen bays, and five veterans with a hundred years of collision work between them [[OBSERVED]].
Nearly six hundred customers rating you five stars [[OBSERVED]].

You told a trade paper the thing most owners will not say aloud: that you are the dominant shop in a town of ten thousand, that you never take it for granted, and that a consolidator could show up any day [[BENCHMARK]].

proposal.heading: What we propose
proposal.lead: The proposal: the count (operations performed against billed, by insurer, with every short pay), the line (your not-included operations and the proof each needs, on every estimate), and the thirty-day result; fixed fee between $1,500 and $2,500; read-only; no customer or vehicle identity leaves the building.

ledger.title: What one repair's unbilled lines look like
ledger.label: Illustrative, not Loren's Body Shop data
ledger.note: Priced at an illustrative $72 door rate. The never-asked shares are the survey's, where it publishes one; every hour and dollar is invented to show the format.

proposal.promise: If your records show our printed range overstated your exposure, our findings letter says so in those words.

sources: Collision Advice and CRASH Network, Who Pays for What? surveys, 2026.
